entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen23447" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23448" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23449" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23449" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23448" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23450" type="x-p"/> The psalmist praises God for his goodness, <reference osisRef="Psa.144.1">Psa 144:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.144.2">Psa 144:2</reference>. Exclamations relative to the vanity of human life, <reference osisRef="Psa.144.3">Psa 144:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.144.4">Psa 144:4</reference>. He prays against his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.144.5-Psa.144.8">Psa 144:5-8</reference>; and extols God's mercy for the temporal blessings enjoyed by his people, <reference osisRef="Psa.144.9-Psa.144.15">Psa 144:9-15</reference>. <div eID="gen23450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23451" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew, and all the Versions, attribute this Psalm to David. The Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic, term it, A Psalm of David against Goliath. The Syriac says, "A Psalm of David when he slew Asaph, the brother of Goliath." Calmet thinks, and with much probability, that it was composed by David after the death of Absalom, and the restoration of the kingdom to peace and tranquillity. From a collation of this with Psalm 18, of which it appears to be an abridgment, preserving the same ideas, and the same forms of expression, there can be no doubt of both having proceeded from the same pen, and that David was the author. There is scarcely an expression here of peculiar importance that is not found in the prototype; and for explanation I must refer generally to the above Psalm. <div eID="gen23451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23452" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23453" type="x-p"/> Teacheth my hands to war - To use sword, battle-axe, or spear. <div eID="gen23453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23454" type="x-p"/> And my fingers to fight - To use the bow and arrows, and the sling.
entries.content_plain: Introduction The psalmist praises God for his goodness, Psa 144:1 , Psa 144:2 . Exclamations relative to the vanity of human life, Psa 144:3 , Psa 144:4 . He prays against his enemies, Psa 144:5-8 ; and extols God's mercy for the temporal blessings enjoyed by his people, Psa 144:9-15 . The Hebrew, and all the Versions, attribute this Psalm to David. The Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic, term it, A Psalm of David against Goliath. The Syriac says, "A Psalm of David when he slew Asaph, the brother of Goliath." Calmet thinks, and with much probability, that it was composed by David after the death of Absalom, and the restoration of the kingdom to peace and tranquillity. From a collation of this with Psalm 18, of which it appears to be an abridgment, preserving the same ideas, and the same forms of expression, there can be no doubt of both having proceeded from the same pen, and that David was the author. There is scarcely an expression here of peculiar importance that is not found in the prototype; and for explanation I must refer generally to the above Psalm. entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23456" type="x-p"/> Lord, what is man - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Psa.8.4">Psa 8:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.8.5">Psa 8:5</reference>. What is Adam, that thou approvest of him? Can he do any thing worthy of thy notice? Or the son of feeble perishing man, that thou shouldest hold him in repute? What care, love, and attention, dost thou lavish upon him!

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23457" type="x-p"/> Man is like to vanity - אדם להבל דמה Adam lahebel damah, literally, Adam is like to Abel, exposed to the same miseries, accidents, and murderers; for in millions of cases the hands of brothers are lifted up to shed the blood of brothers. What are wars but fratricide in the great human family? <div eID="gen23457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23458" type="x-p"/> His days are as a shadow - The life of Abel was promissory of much blessedness; but it afforded merely the shadow of happiness. He was pure and holy, beloved of his parents, and beloved of God; but, becoming the object of his brother's envy, his life became a sacrifice to his piety.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23463" type="x-p"/> He that giveth salvation unto kings - Monarchy, in the principle, is from God: it is that form of government which, in the course of the Divine providence, has principally prevailed; and that which, on the whole, has been most beneficial to mankind. God, therefore, has it under his peculiar protection. It is by him that kings reign; and by his special providence they are protected.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen23463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23464" type="x-p"/> That our sons may be as plants - God had promised to his people, being faithful, Three descriptions of Blessings, <reference osisRef="Deu.28.4">Deu 28:4</reference>. <div eID="gen23464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23465" type="x-p"/> 1. The fruit of the body - sons and daughters. <div eID="gen23465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23466" type="x-p"/> 2. The fruits of the ground - grass and corn in sufficient plenty. <div eID="gen23466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23467" type="x-p"/> 3. Fruit of the cattle-"the increase of kine, and flocks of sheep." <div eID="gen23467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23468" type="x-p"/> These are the blessings to wnich the psalmist refers here, as those in which he might at present exult and triumph: blessings actually enjoyed by his people at large; proofs of his mild and paternal government, and of the especial blessing of the Almighty. The people who there in such a state, and revolted, had no excuse: they were doubly guilty, as ungrateful both to God and man.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen23468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23469" type="x-p"/> That our garners, etc. - Our garners are full. These are not prayers put up by David for such blessings: but assertions, that such blessings were actually in possession. All these expressions should be understood in the present tense. <div eID="gen23469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23470" type="x-p"/> Ten thousands in our streets - בחצתינו bechutsotheynu should be translated in our pens or sheep-walks; for sheep bringing forth in the streets of cities or towns is absurd.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen23470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23471" type="x-p"/> Our oxen may be strong to labor - We have not only an abundance of cattle; but they are of the most strong and vigorous breed. <div eID="gen23471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23472" type="x-p"/> No breaking in - So well ordered is the police of the kingdom, that there are no depredations, no robbers, house-breakers, or marauding parties, in the land; no sudden incursions of neighboring tribes or banditti breaking into fields or houses, carrying away property, and taking with them the people to sell them into captivity: there is no such breaking in, and no such going out, in the nation. My enemies are either become friends, and are united with me in political interests; or are, through fear, obliged to stand aloof.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen23472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23473" type="x-p"/> Happy is that people - "O how happy are the people!" Such were his people; and they had not only all this secular happiness, but they had Jehovah for their God; and in him had a ceaseless fountain of strength, protection, earthly blessings, and eternal mercies! A people in such a case to rebel, must have the curse of God and man.  <chapter eID="Ps.144"/> <div eID="gen23473" type="x-p"/>
